title: Tuvan throat singing
hook: Singers from Tuva can sing two notes at once with a single voice.
peek: In the Republic of Tuva, in southern Siberia, singers hold a deep, steady note while a high, whistling melody floats above it. Both come from the same throat. The trick lies in shaping the mouth to amplify sounds hidden inside every voice.
lede: Tuva is a small republic in southern Siberia, between Russia's forests and the Mongolian steppe. Its singers practise khoomei, a style in which one person produces two or more pitches at the same moment: a low, humming drone and, above it, a clear whistling tune. To listeners hearing it for the first time, it sounds like two people singing.

bullets.text: Any sung note is really a stack of tones: the main pitch plus fainter harmonics at higher frequencies. Normally we hear them blended into one sound, which gives each voice its character.

Throat singers move the tongue, lips and jaw to make the mouth resonate at exactly one harmonic, boosting it until it rings out as a separate note. Shifting to neighbouring harmonics turns those boosted tones into a melody over the drone.

Tuvans name several styles. Sygyt, meaning whistling, has a bright melody high above the drone. Kargyraa is deep and growling, made partly by vibrating tissue above the vocal cords to add a note far below the singer's ordinary voice.

Tuvan ensembles such as Huun-Huur-Tu began touring abroad in the 1990s, bringing the sound to festivals and recordings worldwide. Related styles are sung in neighbouring Mongolia, where the art is recognised by UNESCO.
